section.title: Choose career moves for the capabilities they build
section.deck: An engineering leader traces a research-to-CTO path and explains why directing managers, earning trust, and adapting to company growth required new skills.

blocks.question: Why did you move from research to Facebook?
answer: After five years in a PhD program and three at IBM Research, the guest questioned a mixed research-and-engineering career. He considered academia, quantitative finance, and software engineering, then chose engineering because he wanted to build products affecting many people.

He also wanted engineering to have central status. In his view, finance treated it as supporting another function, while a fast-growing company like Facebook offered both engineering priority and broad impact. These are his reasons for choosing among the opportunities available around 2009, not a general ranking of those professions.

blocks.question: How did the director opportunity at Square arise?
answer: He corrects the host’s premise: he joined Square with a director offer rather than receiving an internal promotion from frontline manager. The team grew from approximately twenty-five to more than fifty people in about a year. Building machine-learning and data infrastructure teams exposed him to a new job: directing through managers rather than directly managing engineers.

blocks.question: What was the biggest skill gap in moving from manager to director?
answer: At Facebook he had become a manager after being an IC, so knowing the team’s technical details gave him authority. At a new company, his reports had longer tenure and knew more than he did. He could no longer justify the extra leadership layer by being the most informed person in the room.

He thinks he performed poorly during roughly the first half-year. Reflection led him toward strategic direction, cross-department resource coordination, and the organization’s hardest problems. The job was to guide an organization toward a better future, rather than reproduce the frontline managers’ work.

Another turning point was understanding what each manager wanted from him. He tried to identify missing capabilities and help them grow toward the next level. That reframed him as someone adding value to their careers.

followups.question: How did you handle managers who hoped to receive the role you were hired into?
answer: He recognized the natural disappointment and tried to demonstrate that his arrival could help their prospects rather than block them. Building trust came first, followed by concrete help with growth and obstacles they could not remove alone. He credits The Five Dysfunctions of a Team with emphasizing trust as the foundation beneath other team behavior.

blocks.question: Is changing companies the best way to move up management levels?
answer: He does not think so; former Facebook colleagues reached very senior roles by staying. His own moves followed a different goal: eventually becoming CTO of an AI company. The intended outcome revealed gaps in infrastructure, frontend work, products, and how an industry business operates.

At Snapchat he could lead data or camera. He deliberately chose camera despite a data and machine-learning background, learning iOS and Android work and spending about two months on iOS study. The product role forced collaboration with product managers and designers that he might not have gained by staying in a familiar backend specialty.

He recalls those first two years as especially happy because he was expanding his knowledge every day. The lesson is to choose an opportunity for the capability it supplies, rather than infer that any external title increase is a sound strategy.

blocks.question: How much must an engineering leader know the team’s details?
answer: Facebook’s bootcamp impressed him: even a newly hired VP fixed bugs and submitted code alongside other hires. He adopted the belief that engineering leadership should remain technical. He still writes and reviews code, mentioning several pull requests a week, and wants enough detail to make sound strategic judgments rather than speak without understanding.

followups.question: How do you balance technical depth with higher-leverage leadership work?
answer: At the start of a week, he identifies the three most important outcomes and concentrates there. Sometimes learning implementation detail is one of those outcomes; other weeks it is not. Recalibrating priorities toward his broader goal matters more than repeating the same activity or simply adding hours. Time is finite, so the key is allocation.

blocks.question: How did Los Angeles differ from Silicon Valley?
answer: Snapchat itself felt surprisingly similar to Facebook’s fast-moving culture, partly because early employees came from established technology centers. The wider city offered a more varied social environment than the technology-heavy conversations he remembered from the Bay Area. Neighbors in unrelated professions helped him consider users outside technology and AI circles. A captioned neighbor’s job title is uncertain, so it is not specified here.

blocks.question: What drove your organization’s growth to about 250 engineers?
answer: He relates the team’s growth to Snapchat’s overall expansion from approximately one hundred employees to three thousand in two years, while crediting recruiting and interviewer effort. Rapid growth was also painful: a culture that works for one hundred people differs from one for three thousand. He likens each doubling to building a new company. Leaders need to adapt instead of insisting that an earlier organizational answer remain right indefinitely.

blocks.question: What did you learn from working with Evan Spiegel?
answer: He recalls an unusually high product-quality bar, down to pixel-level issues in demos. His team learned to bring a genuinely polished demonstration, and he compares that attention with the familiar image of Steve Jobs.

He also describes a leader who valued personal relationships and kept promises. One story is Spiegel telling another leader not to fire the first fifteen engineers because of their founding contribution. Another is returning to the small house associated with Snapchat’s beginnings for board meetings. These are the guest’s accounts of leadership and loyalty, not a recommended universal employment rule.

blocks.question: How were you recruited into later leadership roles?
answer: He says opportunities came inbound through recruiters or personal connections rather than an active search. He preferred people he knew because companies inevitably face both good and difficult periods. He wanted partners he could trust and think with through downturns. Building a professional network early made those later opportunities possible, though his personal inbound experience should not be assumed for every candidate.

blocks.question: How do you compare leadership offers when company size and titles differ?
answer: He does not primarily rank valuation or reporting headcount. In fact, he says he would welcome fewer direct reports. The central test is whether the work brings him closer to the product-building outcome he wants.

Titles belong to a company’s structure and can lose significance when someone leaves. He would rather be known for making a useful product than for holding a senior label. He imagines a very small team building an extremely valuable company, but presents that as an aspiration and prediction rather than an established requirement.

When hiring for his startup, he wants candidates both to believe a large outcome is possible and understand that its probability may be very low. The small probability is a candid framing of startup risk, not a measured forecast.

followups.question: Why tell candidates that the chance of success is low?
answer: He wants people to choose the challenge consciously so normal difficulties do not immediately overturn their expectations. Transparency helps identify the subset of engineers who want the journey, rather than persuade everyone. His battlefield analogy emphasizes preparation for uncertainty and shared commitment.

blocks.question: What are the benefits and costs of using a personal north star instead of money or level?
answer: He sees no universally right criterion. His research colleagues could have successful conventional careers. His own test is future regret: if, fifteen years later, he would regret never trying an AI company, he would rather try now. The goal aligns with his motivation, but he acknowledges that it can create a less conventional path.

blocks.question: What do you regret or wish you had changed?
answer: If he had known he would choose software engineering, he might not have taken the PhD route, though it taught him valuable things. He cannot predict ten years of change—and says even the next few months of AI are uncertain—so he emphasizes adaptability rather than wishing for perfect foresight. Difficult transitions from research to engineering or manager to director can be periods of adjustment, not proof of permanent failure.

blocks.question: How much management growth is situational rather than controllable?
answer: Management roles are constrained by the organization’s needs and structure, which depend on company strategy. He increasingly accepts that he cannot control much of the timing. Doing excellent work in the current role is within his control; promotion is a later signal shaped by other conditions.

He criticizes treating the next level’s bullet points as a contract guaranteeing promotion once checked. That makes happiness dependent on an outcome the person cannot fully command. His alternative is impact now and movement toward work one wants over the long term, while remaining open to later opportunities or founding a company.

blocks.question: What would you tell yourself just after your PhD?
answer: Conventional wisdom need not decide a unique person’s path. He recalls choosing Carnegie Mellon over more broadly prestigious alternatives because of computer science, and leaving research for a small Facebook when few research peers would have done so. An unfamiliar route is less comfortable, but he believes independent thinking can reveal opportunities others miss. The advice follows from his goals rather than asserting that every unconventional choice wins.

blocks.question: What is your current company trying to build?
answer: The guest describes HeyGen as a human-centered video-generation platform aimed at everyday content professionals such as marketers and salespeople, rather than only film production. He emphasizes quality, consistency, controllability, and communicating across languages. His ambition is to make visual storytelling possible without a camera. These are the founder-side product claims and aspirations given in the interview, retained as context for the AI-company goal.
